text: Hi, my name is Bread. I'm a big coffee lover, so I guess I'll start there. I can't really start my day without a cup of coffee, and this morning was no different. I had one before I came to take this test, and I'm already looking forward to another one once it's over. I work in IT at Samsung Heavy Industries. I'm in charge of our IT systems, so my days are pretty busy. I live in an apartment with my wife, and we're pretty much homebodies. In my free time, I like listening to music, playing computer games, and reading. So, yeah, that's me in a nutshell: coffee, my wife, and my computer. I'm happy to be here, and I hope I do well today!

Koreans are really into fashion. People dress up even for a quick trip to the grocery store. In the city, you'll see a lot of trendy outfits, like oversized jackets, wide-leg pants, and white sneakers. Young people follow K-pop idols' styles, so whatever a famous singer wears, it sells out in a day. Another special feature is that we dress for the weather. In the winter, almost everyone wears a long padded coat. In the summer, people carry a small fan or an umbrella for the sun. And in the office, it's pretty common to wear business casual. Overall, I'd say Koreans care a lot about how they look.

I like to keep it simple and comfortable. On weekends, I usually wear a hoodie, jeans, and sneakers. I'm not a fashion guy at all, so I just go for comfort. At work, we have a business casual dress code, so I wear a collared shirt and slacks. Today, I'm wearing a light blue shirt and a navy jacket, since it's a fall day. I wanted to look decent for this test! I also wore my most comfortable shoes, because I didn't want to be nervous and uncomfortable at the same time. My wife says I wear the same thing every day. She's probably right.

When I was younger, baggy jeans were super popular. Everyone wore big sweatshirts with huge logos, and sneakers with thick soles. I remember begging my sisters to let me borrow their clothes. I had six older sisters, so I got a lot of hand-me-downs! It wasn't exactly cool. These days, the trends are different. Skinny jeans came and went, and now we've come full circle, because baggy and oversized are back again! Also, people love athleisure, like yoga pants and running jackets, even outside the gym. It's funny how fashion always repeats itself. I'm just glad my old clothes are back in style!

The park I often go to is a seaside park near my apartment here in Geoje. It's about a 10-minute walk from my home. It's a long, narrow park along the coast, with a walking path, big old trees, and lots of benches facing the sea. In the middle, there's a small playground and a little plaza where people exercise or have picnics. From the benches, you can see ships and islands. In the spring, the cherry blossoms are gorgeous. I go there about once a week, usually in the evening with my wife. We take a walk and chat. It's the perfect place to unwind after a long day at work.

I first got into parks when my kids were little. Eunbin and Suhyun had so much energy, and our apartment was too small for them to run around. So every weekend, we took them to the park to burn off their energy. At first, I only went because I had to. I'd sit on a bench with my coffee and watch them play. But over time, I started to enjoy it myself. The fresh air and the quiet were so relaxing. Now the kids are older, so I mostly go with my wife. Instead of watching the kids, we walk and talk. My interest has changed from "a place for the kids" to "my own place to recharge". I think it'll keep changing as I get older.

One experience I'll never forget happened last fall. My wife and I were taking our usual evening walk when we heard music coming from the plaza. A small crowd had gathered, and a group of amateur musicians was playing live. They were singing old Korean pop songs, and people were clapping along. We sat on a bench with two cups of hot coffee, and we just listened. Then suddenly, the singer pointed at us and said, "Come on up and dance!" I froze. I'm the least dancy person in the world. But my wife grabbed my hand, and before I knew it, I was in front of everyone. I danced like a robot, and the crowd went wild! I was so embarrassed, but it was a blast. It was memorable because it was so unexpected, and my wife still has the video. She shows it to everyone!

We have all kinds of hotels in Korea, from luxury five-star hotels to small, budget-friendly ones. In big cities like Seoul and Busan, most hotels are located downtown, near train stations, shopping areas, or tourist spots. They're usually clean, modern, and very convenient. In resort areas, like Jeju or the east coast, there are big resort hotels with ocean views and swimming pools. We also have a unique kind of stay: traditional Korean houses called "hanok", which have been turned into hotels. And a lot of hotels have free breakfast buffets, which I love. Compared to other countries, I'd say Korean hotels are very clean and the service is excellent.

The last time I stayed at a hotel was in Busan, about two months ago. My wife and I took a weekend trip to Haeundae Beach. We stayed at a hotel with an ocean view. When we checked in, the room was on a high floor, and the view was amazing. I just stood at the window for a few minutes. After we dropped off our bags, we went out to eat seafood and walk on the beach. Back at the hotel, we spent time at the rooftop pool, which was really relaxing. The next morning, we had a big breakfast buffet, and I had three cups of coffee. Then we checked out. It was short, but it was just what we needed.

A hotel I'll never forget is a hanok hotel in Jeonju. A hanok is a traditional Korean house, with a wooden floor and paper doors. I stayed there with my wife a few years ago. It was totally different from a normal hotel. The room had a heated floor called "ondol", so we slept on thick blankets on the floor. I thought I wouldn't sleep well, but I slept like a baby! In the morning, the owner served us a traditional breakfast in the courtyard, with rice, soup, and lots of side dishes. We drank hot tea and listened to the birds. It felt like we'd gone back in time. It was special to me because it was so peaceful, and it made me appreciate Korean culture.

Hey, it's me. Thanks for inviting me to your birthday party! I'm really looking forward to it. I have a few questions about the location. First, what's the name of the bar?. Okay. And where exactly is it? Is it near a subway station or a bus stop?. Got it. What time does the party start?. Also, is there parking nearby, or should I take a taxi?. One last thing: do I need to make a reservation, or is it already booked?. Perfect. I'll see you there, and I'll bring a gift! Happy early birthday!

Hey, it's me. I'm so sorry, but I have some bad news. I can't make it to your birthday party. I just found out that I have an important test tomorrow, a certification exam for work, and I haven't studied enough. I feel terrible, because I really wanted to celebrate with you. But I have a few ideas. First, how about I come for just an hour before it gets late, so I can at least say happy birthday? If that doesn't work, I could take you out for dinner the day after my test. Or I could send you a gift and a cake to the bar, so the party doesn't miss me! Which one sounds best to you? Again, I'm so sorry. I'll make it up to you. Dinner's on me!

Yes, I have. A few months ago, my father-in-law and I made plans to play golf together. He's 80, but he's a better golfer than I am! We booked a tee time and I was really looking forward to it. But the night before, it started pouring rain, and the forecast said it wouldn't stop. I called him early in the morning, and he said, "A little rain never hurt anyone!" But I knew we couldn't play in that weather, and I didn't want him to catch a cold at his age. So I suggested a plan B: screen golf! It's an indoor golf simulator, and it's very popular in Korea. At first, he wasn't thrilled, but he agreed. We ended up having a great time, and he beat me by ten strokes. Afterward, we had lunch together. It turned out to be a better day than I'd expected. Sometimes plan B is even better than plan A.

I think traveling abroad is a lot easier now. When I took my first trip abroad, I had to buy paper tickets, carry a thick guidebook, and exchange cash at the airport. These days, I can do almost everything on my phone. I book flights and hotels online, use a translation app, and pay with my card. Plus, there are more cheap flights, so more people can afford to travel. Last winter, my family and I went to Da Nang, in Vietnam, and we planned the entire trip on our phones. On the other hand, there are some downsides. Popular places get really crowded. Prices have gone up, and airports are busy. Also, because everyone posts photos on social media, it's harder to find hidden gems. But overall, I'd say it's easier, and it's a lot more fun.

There are a few things that are important when people travel abroad. First, safety. People want to feel safe, so they buy travel insurance and keep copies of their passports. Second, food. Everyone wants to try the local specialties. Third, sightseeing. People are interested in seeing famous landmarks, beautiful beaches, and old temples or castles. Some people also enjoy local markets and festivals. As for what travelers should do, I'd say they should respect the local culture. Learn a few basic phrases, like "hello" and "thank you". It goes a long way. It's also a good idea to plan ahead. My daughter Eunbin is great at this. For our Da Nang trip, she made a detailed schedule, and everything went smoothly. And finally, stay open-minded. Things won't always go as planned, but that's part of the adventure.
